themes.description: Users trust the companion more when it admits uncertainty or acknowledges mistakes, rather than presenting only correct answers.
themes.insight: Users report higher trust when the navigation companion admits uncertainty or owns its mistakes, while repeated errors or lack of honest cues reduce trust.
themes.caveat: The evidence comes from a limited number of interview transcripts, so it may not represent broader user populations.

quotes.title: Transcript 2
quotes.text: Honestly I only trust the companion when it admits it is unsure. It once said it could not find the lab and asked me to look for a sign, and that made me trust it more.

quotes.title: Text 1
quotes.text: A good companion speaks rarely, shows the next step only, and owns its mistakes. Trust is built less by accuracy than by honest uncertainty.

quotes.title: Transcript 3
quotes.text: But when it gave me the wrong turn twice I stopped believing it. I wish I could switch off the chatter in quiet places like the reading room.

themes.theme: Cognitive load from visual and auditory clutter
themes.description: Frequent overlays, pop‑ups, and misheard voice instructions distract users and cause them to look away or revert to simpler cues.
themes.insight: Frequent visual overlays and excessive voice instructions distract users, causing them to look away, stop listening, or dismiss the companion.
themes.caveat: The evidence comes only from a small number of self‑reported experiences and does not include objective measures of cognitive load.

quotes.title: Text 1
quotes.text: Navigation aids in mixed reality fail when they compete for attention. Designers keep adding overlays, but pedestrians need a calm view of the real street.

quotes.title: Transcript 1
quotes.text: The first time [participant] showed me the companion, it talked too much and I stopped listening.

quotes.title: Transcript 2
quotes.text: Too many pop-ups pull my attention away from the corridor and I nearly walked into a glass door.

quotes.title: Text 2
quotes.text: One participant stopped mid-corridor to dismiss a notification.

themes.description: Wearing a heavy headset in public draws attention, makes users feel self‑conscious, and can cause physical discomfort such as dizziness.
themes.insight: Wearing a heavy mixed‑reality headset in public makes users feel self‑conscious because people stare, and it can cause physical discomfort such as dizziness.
themes.caveat: The evidence comes from a limited set of participant comments and cannot indicate how common these experiences are across a broader population.

quotes.title: Transcript 3
quotes.text: [participant] from my hostel said the glasses made him dizzy. People stare when I speak to it, so I mostly use the arrows.

quotes.title: Text 1
quotes.text: Wearing a heavy headset in public also carries a social cost, because people react to what they cannot see.

quotes.title: Transcript 2
quotes.text: I would feel silly talking to a companion in front of other people. At home it feels fine, in a crowded lobby it does not.

themes.description: Participants favor arrows they can glance at over voice instructions, and report fatigue from small text or prolonged headset use.
themes.insight: Participants prefer glanceable arrow cues over voice instructions, and they experience visual fatigue from small text and physical fatigue from wearing the headset for extended periods.
themes.caveat: The findings are based on a small pilot study with only a few participants, limiting generalizability.

quotes.title: Transcript 1
quotes.text: I wear the headset when I walk through a new campus building because the arrows on the floor save me from stopping every minute.

quotes.title: Text 2
quotes.text: In the pilot, two of three participants returned to arrows after the voice mode misheard place names. Observers saw frequent glances at the floor and at phones.

quotes.title: Transcript 2
quotes.text: [participant] told me that voice instructions work better for her, but I prefer arrows because I can glance at them. The device is heavy after twenty minutes.

quotes.title: Transcript 1
quotes.text: After a long walk my eyes get tired and the small text is hard to read.

themes.description: The navigation companion reduces feelings of isolation by greeting users by name and providing a sense of companionship during exploration.
themes.insight: The navigation companion reduces feelings of isolation by greeting users by name and offering a sense of companionship during exploration.
themes.caveat: The evidence is based only on a few transcript excerpts, so it may not represent broader user experiences.

quotes.title: Transcript 3
quotes.text: As a new student I felt isolated in the first week and the companion gave me a reason to explore. It remembered where the library was and greeted me by name, which felt friendly.
